title: Titration calculations
examples: How do I calculate the moles of the unknown substance?
What does the equivalence point actually mean in titration?
Can I use the volume of the indicator to find the concentration?

explain.say: Today we learn about titration calculations in chemistry.

items: It uses a known standard solution.
The endpoint helps determine the reaction.

explain.say: First we look at concordant titres in titrations.
Next we connect moles to concentration using formulas.
Remember that concentration is moles per unit volume.
For a real-life example consider blood testing in a lab.
A common mistake is mixing up the units when calculating.

items: Always ensure volume is in liters.
If given milliliters, divide by one hundred.
Moles must match the volume units.

faq.q: What are concordant titres used for in titration?
faq.a: Concordant titres are very close titre volumes recorded during a titration.
asks: Why do we need to check titres?

faq.q: How do I convert moles to concentration?
faq.a: Concentration is found by dividing the number of moles by the total volume in liters.
asks: What is the formula for concentration?
Do I use the total volume or the added volume?

faq.q: If my titres are not concordant, what should I do?
faq.a: You should carefully check your equipment and repeat the titration process.
asks: What does it mean if my titres vary a lot?

faq.q: Must the volume always be in liters for concentration?
faq.a: Yes, for standard calculations, the volume must be in liters to get the correct molarity.
asks: Can I use milliliters for concentration?
What units should the volume be in?

faq.q: What is the purpose of the endpoint in titration?
faq.a: The endpoint is the point where the indicator changes colour, signalling the reaction is complete.
asks: Is the endpoint the same as the equivalence point?
How do I know when the reaction has finished?

facts: Concentration is often measured in moles per litre, or molarity.
Concordant titres are a measure of precision in titration.
The relationship is concentration equals moles divided by volume.
Titration helps determine the unknown concentration of a solution.

quiz.say: A student titrates 25 millilitres of acid with a standard base solution. If the moles of base used were 0 point 02 moles, what is the concentration of the base?
quiz.why: You divide the moles, 0 point 02, by the volume in litres, 0 point 25, to get 0 point 08.

wrong.0: This is the volume used, forgetting to divide by the moles.
wrong.2: This is the value of the moles, forgetting to divide by the volume.
wrong.3: This happens if you incorrectly divide the moles by 500 instead of 0 point 25.

quiz.say: If three titres are 22.1 millilitres, 22.3 millilitres, and 22.0 millilitres, what is the best estimate for the titre volume?
quiz.why: You calculate the average of the three recorded titres for the most accurate result.

wrong.0: This only uses the last recorded titre, ignoring the others.
wrong.1: This only uses the first recorded titre, which might be an outlier.
wrong.2: This incorrectly adds the three titres together instead of finding the average.

quiz.say: A sample has 0 point 015 moles of substance X. If this sample was diluted to a final volume of 50 millilitres, what is its concentration?
quiz.why: You convert 50 millilitres to 0 point 05 litres, then divide 0 point 015 by 0 point 05.

wrong.0: This forgets to account for the final volume of the solution.
wrong.1: This incorrectly divides the moles by the number 50 instead of the volume in litres.
wrong.2: This happens if you divide 0 point 015 by 10 litres instead of 0 point 05 litres.
